content: Data should be analyzed and presented in a manner that enables all relevant stakeholders to interpret it effectively during strategic review meetings. A mid-term review of the strategic plan implementation is recommended, especially for plans spanning five years or more. This review should be incorporated into the strategic plan, with necessary resources allocated in the budget. The objectives of the mid-term review include: Assessing whether the country is on track to achieve the strategic plan targets. Identifying bottlenecks in implementation that need to be addressed to accelerate progress. Highlighting good practices that can be scaled up. Identifying emerging challenges, threats, and opportunities, and updating the strategic plan if necessary. If significant modifications to the National Strategic Plan (NSP) are required based on the mid-term review, these changes can be documented as an addendum to the strategic plan. This addendum should be formally endorsed by the relevant government authorities whenever possible. An end-term review is conducted during the final year of the strategic plan’s implementation. This serves as a baseline for preparing the successor strategic plan. It is a comprehensive exercise involving all stakeholders in the plan’s implementation. The review should be planned, costed, and budgeted as part of the strategic plan. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) components for the NSP include specific indicators, their purposes, calculation methods, sources of information, periodicity, and responsible parties for data collection. Examples include: Goal: TB incidence (measured annually using WHO estimates and modeling). Goal: Number of TB deaths (measured annually using WHO estimates and modeling). Goal: Proportion of TB-affected families facing catastrophic costs (measured through surveys at the end of the NSP period). Objective 1: TB treatment coverage (measured quarterly through surveillance systems). Objective 2: Social protection interventions for TB patients (tracked through the development and publication of intervention packages). Objective 3: Readiness for digital case-based surveillance systems (assessed through readiness reports). Costing for the strategic plan should outline resource needs for implementation. The format for presenting costing should remain flexible to accommodate dynamic stakeholder and funding partner requirements. Contingency planning is essential to address potential risks or events that may disrupt access to TB care and prevention services. Examples of contingency measures include: Engaging community health workers for TB screening and sputum collection. Redirecting specimen transportation systems to operational facilities. Utilizing digital technologies for screening and laboratory result delivery. Ensuring TB services are included in emergency response packages. Monitoring and redistributing supplies to sites with inadequate stock. Implementing multi-month dispensing of anti-TB drugs. These measures should involve national and subnational staff, community health workers, technical and funding partners, civil society organizations, and service providers for digital health technologies. The strategic plan should also include standard operating procedures (SOPs) and tools to support routine quality checks and data validation at all administrative levels. Workshops for data analysis and use should be conducted annually at the provincial level to enhance M&E capacity. References include WHO guidelines, global TB reports, and various frameworks and tools for strategic planning, monitoring, and evaluation.
